x: Commentary on Sūrat ʿAbasa (He Frowned). In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Commentary on the saying of God, exalted is His praise: ‘He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him. And how would you know? Perhaps he would purify himself, or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him.’ By ‘He frowned,’ God means he contracted his face in aversion; ‘and turned away’ means that he turned aside; ‘because the blind man came to him’ means because the blind man came. It is reported that some reciters lengthened the alif in ‘because he came,’ reading it as a question: ‘Was it because the blind man came that he frowned and turned away?’ as some read ‘because he had wealth and sons’
r
with a lengthened alif in an. It is reported that the blind man mentioned in this verse was Ibn Umm Maktūm, and the Prophet was admonished on his account.

m: Reports concerning this were related to us.

c: Saʿīd ibn Yaḥyā al-Umawī related to us, from his father, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from ʿUrwah, from ʿĀʾishah, who said:
m: ‘He frowned and turned away’ was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktūm. He came to the Messenger of God and kept saying, ‘Guide me.’ The Messenger of God had some of the leading polytheists with him. The Prophet turned away from the blind man and attended to the other man… …and said, ‘Do you see any harm in what I am saying?’ He replied, ‘No.’ It was concerning this that ‘He frowned and turned away’ was revealed.

c: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, from his father, from his uncle, from his father, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him’: While the Messenger of God was speaking privately with ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, and al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib—he often approached them, hoping they would believe—a blind man named ʿAbd Allāh ibn Umm Maktūm came toward him while he was speaking with them. ʿAbd Allāh asked the Prophet to recite a verse of the Qurʾan and said, ‘Messenger of God, teach me from what God has taught you.’ The Messenger of God turned away from him, frowned, and disliked his interruption, attending instead to the others. When the Messenger of God finished and began returning home, God partially took away his sight; he bowed his head, and then God revealed these verses. When they were revealed concerning him, the Messenger of God honored and spoke kindly to him, saying, ‘What do you need? Is there anything you want?’ Whenever he left, the Prophet would ask, ‘Do you need anything?’ This was after God revealed, ‘As for the one who considers himself self-sufficient, you attend to him, though it is no concern of yours if he does not purify himself.’

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Hishām, from his father, who said:
m: It was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktūm… …‘He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him.’

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid,
m: concerning ‘because the blind man came to him’: he was a man from Banū Fihr called Ibn Umm Maktūm.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: concerning the verse: He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zāʾidah, Ibn Umm Maktūm. He came asking the Prophet to recite to him while the Prophet was speaking privately with Umayyah ibn Khalaf, one of Quraysh’s notables. God’s Prophet turned away from him, and God revealed what you hear, from ‘He frowned and turned away’ through ‘you are distracted from him.’ We were told that afterward the Prophet appointed him twice as his deputy over Medina while he went on military expeditions, and he led its people in prayer.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said
m: he saw him at al-Qādisiyyah carrying a black banner and wearing armor.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, who said:
m: Ibn Umm Maktūm came to the Prophet while he was speaking with Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The Prophet turned away from him, and God revealed ‘He frowned and turned away.’ Thereafter the Prophet honored him. Anas said: I saw him at al-Qādisiyyah wearing armor and carrying a black banner.

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us that he heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say concerning ‘He frowned and turned away’: The Messenger of God was attending to a wealthy man from the Quraysh polytheists, hoping he would believe. A blind man from the Anṣār named ʿAbd Allāh ibn Umm Maktūm came and began asking the Prophet. The Prophet disliked it and turned away, attending instead to the rich man. God admonished His Prophet, who thereafter honored Ibn Umm Maktūm and appointed him twice as his deputy over Medina during military expeditions.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd, whom I asked about this verse, as saying: Ibn Umm Maktūm came to the Messenger of God, led by a guide who could see while he could not. The Messenger of God was signaling to the guide to restrain him, while Ibn Umm Maktūm pressed forward without seeing. The Messenger of God frowned, and God admonished him, revealing these verses through ‘you are distracted from him.’ Ibn Zayd said: It was said that if the Messenger of God had ever concealed any revelation, he would have concealed this one from himself. In his pre-Islamic days, he had attended to that prominent man hoping he would accept Islam, and so was distracted from this man.

evidence.text: It is reported that some reciters lengthened the alif in ‘because he came,’ reading it as a question: ‘Was it because the blind man came that he frowned and turned away?’ as some read ‘because he had wealth and sons’ [68:14] with a lengthened alif in an.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And how would you know? Perhaps he would purify himself’: God, exalted is His mention, says to His Prophet Muḥammad: How would you know? Perhaps… …this blind man whose face you frowned at will purify himself—that is, cleanse himself of his sins.

c: Ibn Zayd’s explanation was related to me
m: by Yūnus, who said Ibn Wahb informed us that Ibn Zayd said ‘perhaps he will purify himself’ means ‘perhaps he will accept Islam.’

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him’: that is, he may remember and the reminder may benefit him; he may take heed, and reflection and admonition may benefit him. The reading with ‘benefit’ in the indicative case is coordinated with ‘remember.’ It is also reported that ʿĀṣim read it both in the subjunctive and indicative. The subjunctive makes it the response to laʿalla (‘perhaps’) with the fāʾ, as in the poet’s verse: ‘Perhaps the vicissitudes of time, or their turns, will return to us one of its dark locks, so that the soul may rest from its sighs and the thirst may be quenched from its burning.’ The verb ‘be quenched’ is also reported in both indicative and subjunctive forms.

evidence.text: The reading with ‘benefit’ in the indicative case is coordinated with ‘remember.’
It is also reported that ʿĀṣim read it both in the subjunctive and indicative.

x: Commentary on God’s saying: ‘As for the one who considers himself self-sufficient, you attend to him, though it is no concern of yours if he does not purify himself. But as for the one who comes to you striving, while he fears God, you are distracted from him.’ God says to His Prophet Muḥammad: As for the one who considers himself self-sufficient through wealth, you turn your attention to him, hoping he will accept Islam.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, who said:
m: ‘As for the one who considers himself self-sufficient, you attend to him’ was revealed concerning al-ʿAbbās.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: the one who considered himself self-sufficient was ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah and Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah. ‘Though it is no concern of yours if he does not purify himself’ means: what responsibility is it of yours if he does not cleanse himself of unbelief and accept Islam? ‘As for the one who comes to you striving, while he fears God’ means this blind man who came to you earnestly and fears and reveres God. ‘You are distracted from him’ means that you turn away from him, occupy yourself with someone else, and neglect him.

x: Commentary on God’s saying: ‘No indeed! It is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it, in honored sheets, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and righteous. Cursed be man! How ungrateful he is!’ God says: No, Muḥammad, the matter is not as you are doing—frowning at the one who comes to you striving and fearing God, while turning your attention to the one who considers himself self-sufficient. ‘It is a reminder’ means that this admonition and this sūrah are a reminder, an admonition and lesson. ‘So whoever wills may remember it’… …means that whoever among God’s servants wills may remember it, that is, remember God’s revelation and inspiration. The pronoun in ‘it is a reminder’ refers to the sūrah, while the pronoun in ‘remember it’ refers to the revelation and inspiration. ‘In sheets’ means that it is a reminder in honored sheets; ‘exalted and purified’ refers to the Preserved Tablet, which is exalted and pure with God.
Regarding His saying, ‘In the hands of scribes’: the honored sheets are in the hands of safarah, the plural of sāfir.
The interpreters differed over who they are.
Some said they are scribes.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘in the hands of scribes’: they are writers.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, who said
m: they are scribes.

x: Others said they are reciters.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: concerning ‘whoever wills may remember it, in honored sheets, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes’… …he said they are reciters.

x: Others said they are angels.

c: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, through his father and uncle, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘in the hands of scribes, noble and righteous’: they are angels.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying: the scribes are those who enumerate deeds. The soundest view is that they are angels who carry revelation between God and His messengers. A people’s envoy is one who goes between them to make peace; one says safartu bayna al-qawmi when one reconciles them. A poet said: ‘I do not abandon mediation among my people, nor do I walk deceitfully when I walk.’ This interpretation can encompass the views that they are scribes or reciters, since angels read the books and carry messages between God and His messengers.

evidence.text: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, concerning ‘whoever wills may remember it, in honored sheets, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes’… …he said they are reciters.
This interpretation can encompass the views that they are scribes or reciters, since angels read the books and carry messages between God and His messengers.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Noble and righteous’: al-bararah is the plural of bārr, just as al-kafarah is the plural of kāfir… …and al-saḥarah is the plural of sāḥir. In ordinary Arabic usage, however, the singular is a man barr and a woman barrāh. In the plural, it returns to the pattern of the plural of an active participle, as with a man sarī and a people sarāh. By analogy the singular would be sārin, though some Arabs have been heard to say ‘a people khayarah bararah.’ The singular of khayarah is khayr, and the singular of bararah is barr.
Regarding His saying, ‘Cursed be man! How ungrateful he is!’ God, exalted is His mention, says: May the unbelieving human being be cursed! How ungrateful he is! Mujāhid said something similar.

c: Mūsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Masrūqī related to me, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd al-Ḥammānī, from al-Aʿmash, from Mujāhid, who said:
m: Whenever the Qurʾan says ‘Cursed be man’ or speaks of something done to man, it refers to the unbeliever.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān:
m: I was told that ‘Cursed be man! How ungrateful he is!’ refers to the unbeliever. There are two possible meanings for ‘how ungrateful’: one is an expression of amazement at his unbelief despite God’s kindnesses and favors to him; the other is the question, ‘What made him an unbeliever?’

x: Commentary on God’s saying: ‘From what thing did He create him? From a sperm-drop He created him and proportioned him. Then He made the way easy for him. Then He caused him to die and had him buried. Then, when He wills, He will raise him. No indeed! He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him.’ God, exalted is His mention, says: From what did his Lord create the unbelieving human being, when he acts proudly and arrogantly toward obedience to his Lord and acknowledgment of His oneness? Then He made clear what He created him from: ‘From a sperm-drop He created him and proportioned him’ through successive stages—a sperm-drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh—until his stages in his mother’s womb were complete. ‘Then He made the way easy for him’ means that He made the path accessible to him.
The interpreters differed over which path He made easy.
Some said it was his exit from his mother’s womb.

c: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, from his father, from his uncle, from his father, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: who explained it as God making his exit from his mother’s womb easy.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Ismāʿīl, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, who said
m: it means the path of the womb.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, who said
m: it means his exit from his mother’s womb.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: who explained ‘Then He made the way easy for him’ as his exit from his mother’s womb.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: with the same explanation.

x: Others said the meaning is that We made clear to him the path of truth and falsehood and taught it to him, making it easy for him to follow.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, who said
m: it is like God’s saying, ‘We showed him the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful’
r

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid,
m: with the same explanation.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: it is the path of wretchedness and happiness, as in ‘Then He made the way easy for him.’

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, who said
m: al-Ḥasan explained it as… …the path of goodness.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying: He guided him to Islam and religion, made it easy for him, and made it known to him; the path is the path of Islam. In my judgment, the sounder of the two interpretations is that He made the path out of his mother’s womb easy for him. We prefer this because it accords more closely with the apparent wording of the verse: the preceding and following statements describe God’s creation of him, the shaping of his body, and his passage through successive stages. It is therefore more fitting that the middle statement match what comes before and after it.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Then He caused him to die and had him buried’: He then took his soul and caused him to die. ‘Had him buried’ means He made him one who has a grave. A qābir is someone who buries the dead with his own hands, as al-Aʿshā said: ‘If she laid a dead man upon her breast, he would live and not be carried to a gravedigger.’ A muqbir is God, who commanded His servants to bury the dead after their death, thus making the person one with a grave. The Arabs say, as I have been told, ‘I cut the camel’s tail,’ while ‘God cut it off’; ‘I broke the bull’s horn,’ while ‘God broke it’; and ‘I drove so-and-so away,’ while ‘God made him an outcast.’

Regarding His saying, ‘Then, when He wills, He will raise him’: when God wills, He will raise him after his death and bring him to life. One says, ‘God raised the dead,’ meaning He revived him; and ‘the dead man rose’ means he came to life himself. Al-Aʿshā said: ‘Until people, seeing it, say: “How wondrous—the dead man has risen!”’

Regarding His saying, ‘No indeed! He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him’: God says: No, the matter is not as this unbelieving person claims—that he has rendered God’s due upon him in himself and his wealth. ‘He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him’ means he has not performed the duties his Lord imposed upon him.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said:
m: No one ever fully discharges all that has been prescribed for him. Al-Ḥārith added: all that has been prescribed for him.

x: Commentary on God’s saying: ‘Let man look at his food: how We poured down water in abundance, then split the earth open, and caused grain to grow in it, and grapes and clover, olives and palms, and gardens dense with trees.’ God, exalted is His mention, says: Let this unbelieving person who denies God’s oneness look at his food and how it was arranged for him.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Mujāhid,
m: concerning ‘Let man look at his food and drink’: he said, ‘his food and drink.’

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: it is a sign for them. The reciters differed over ‘how We poured down water in abundance.’ Most reciters of Medina and Basra read innā with kasrah, as a new sentence. Most reciters of Kufa read annā with fatḥah, making it dependent on ‘let man look at,’ as though the preposition were repeated before it. With fatḥah, it could also be nominative, with the implied sense ‘his food is Our pouring water abundantly.’ The soundest view to me is that both are established readings, and whichever a reciter uses is correct.

evidence.text: The reciters differed over ‘how We poured down water in abundance.’
Most reciters of Medina and Basra read innā with kasrah, as a new sentence.
Most reciters of Kufa read annā with fatḥah, making it dependent on ‘let man look at,’ as though the preposition were repeated before it.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘How We poured down water in abundance’: that is, We sent down rain from the sky in a downpour… …and poured it down upon the earth. ‘Then We split the earth open’: We cleaved and broke it apart with vegetation. ‘And caused grain to grow in it’ means every kind of crop produced by the earth, such as wheat, barley, and other grains. ‘And grapes’ means grapevines. ‘And clover’ means fresh fodder; the people of Mecca call al-qaṭṭ clover.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: who explained clover as al-fiṣfiṣah (alfalfa).

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, who said
m: clover is al-faṣāfiṣ (alfalfa).

x: al-fiṣfiṣah is fresh fodder.

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say that ʿUbayd reported al-Ḍaḥḥāk explaining it as fresh fodder.

c: Bishr related to us, from ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Ziyād, from Yūnus, from al-Ḥasan, who said
m: clover is fodder.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And olives’: these are the olives from which oil is made. ‘And palms and gardens dense with trees’: we have already explained that a garden is an enclosed orchard.

Regarding His saying, ‘Dense with trees’: that is, thick and massive. By ‘dense with trees,’ He means large, thick trees in gardens. Ghulb is the plural of aghlab, a man with a thick neck. Al-Farazdaq said: ‘He roared and roused a thick-necked, lionlike beast—woe to Ibn al-Marāghah for what he stirred up!’
The interpreters explained it similarly, though their descriptions differed.
Some said it refers to trees growing close together.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Ibn Idrīs, from ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: gardens are what grows thick and close together.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: they are intertwined.

x: Others said that gardens refer to all kinds of trees.

c: Abū Hishām related to us, from Ibn Fuḍayl, from ʿĀṣim, from his father, who said:
m: gardens are the growth of every kind of tree.

c: Muḥammad ibn Sinān al-Qazzāz related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from Shabīb, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: that ‘gardens dense with trees’ means trees in Paradise whose shade people enjoy.

x: Others said ghulb means tall.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: it means tall.

x: Others said it refers to noble date palms.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, who said
m: ghulb means noble date palms.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah,
m: with the same explanation.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying: they are large date palms with massive trunks. Ghulb is also said of men with thick necks; one says aghlab al-raqabah, meaning large-necked.
Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from his father, from ʿIkrimah… …who explained ‘gardens dense with trees’ as trees with massive trunks.

x: Commentary on God’s saying: ‘And fruit and fodder, as provision for you and your livestock. Then, when the Deafening Blast comes, the day a person flees from his brother, his mother and father, his wife and children—each of them that day will have a matter to occupy him. Some faces that day will be radiant, laughing, rejoicing; and some faces that day will be covered with dust, veiled by gloom. Those are the unbelievers, the wicked.’ By ‘fruit’ God means what people eat of the fruits of trees; al-abb is the grass and vegetation eaten by livestock.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Mubārak, from al-Ḥasan, who said
m: fruit is what the son of Adam eats.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: fruit is what people eat.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, who said:
m: fruit is for you.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying… …‘Fruit is for us.’

c: Ḥumayd ibn Masʿadah related to us, from Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal, from Ḥumayd, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:
m: ʿUmar recited ‘He frowned and turned away’ until he reached ‘fruit and fodder.’ He said, ‘We know what fruit is, but what is fodder?’ Then, as al-Ṭabarī says, he seems to have said—though he was uncertain—‘This is needless complication.’

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from Ibn Abī ʿAdī, from Ḥumayd, from Anas, who said:
m: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb recited the sūrah. When he reached ‘fruit and fodder,’ he said, ‘We know what fruit is, but what is fodder?’ Then he said, ‘By your life, Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, this is needless complication.’

c: Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, from Shuʿbah, from Mūsā ibn Anas, from Anas, who said:
m: ʿUmar recited ‘fruit and fodder’ with a stick in his hand and said, ‘What is fodder?’ Then he said, ‘What we know is enough,’ and dropped the stick.

c: Ibn al-Muthannā related to us, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar, from Shuʿbah, from Khulayʿd ibn Jaʿfar, from Abū Iyās Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah, from Anas, from ʿUmar, who said:
m: ‘This is needless complication.’

c: Qatādah related to me from Anas, from ʿUmar,
m: with the same account. Abū Kurayb, Abū al-Sāʾib, and Yaʿqūb related to us, saying:

c: Ibn Idrīs related to us, saying:
m: I heard ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who counted seven: He placed his sustenance in seven things and made it from seven. At the end he said: fodder is what the earth grows that people do not eat.

c: Abū Hishām related to us, from Ibn Fuḍayl, from ʿĀṣim, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: fodder is the earth’s growth eaten by animals but not people.

c: Abū Kurayb and Abū al-Sāʾib related to us, from Ibn Idrīs, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said
m: Ibn ʿAbbās counted and said fodder is what the earth grows for livestock. That is Abū Kurayb’s wording; Abū al-Sāʾib’s version says it is what the earth grows that people and livestock eat.

c: Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, through his father and uncle, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: fodder is all herbage and pasture.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from Manṣūr, from Abū Razīn, who said
m: fodder is vegetation.
Ibn Ḥumayd related to us through the same chain with the same wording.

c: Ibn Bashshār related to us, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Sufyān, from al-Aʿmash or another authority, from Mujāhid, who said
m: fodder is pasture.

c: Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, from Mihrān, from Sufyān,
m: who reported Mujāhid’s explanation of ‘fodder’ as pasture.

c: Abū Kurayb related to us, from Wakīʿ, from Mubārak, from al-Ḥasan, who said
m: fodder is what livestock eat.

c: Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, from Abū ʿĀṣim, from ʿĪsā; and al-Ḥārith related to me, from al-Ḥasan, from Warqāʾ—both from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said
m: fodder is what livestock eat.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah, who said:
m: fodder is for your livestock, a succession of blessings from God.

c: Bishr related to us, from ʿAbd al-Wāḥid, from Yūnus, from al-Ḥasan, who said
m: fodder is grass.

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us, from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, who said
m: it is what animals eat.

c: I was told by al-Ḥusayn,
m: who heard Abū Muʿādh say that ʿUbayd reported hearing… …al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain fodder as pasture.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying: fodder is for our livestock; it is what they graze. He recited ‘as provision for you and your livestock.’

c: Ibn Wahb also informed us that
m: Yūnus and ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith reported from Ibn Shihāb that Anas ibn Mālik told him he heard ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb say: God says ‘clover, olives, palms, gardens dense with trees, fruit and fodder.’ We know all of that, but what is fodder? He struck his hand and said—‘By God’ is added in one textual witness—‘this is needless complication. Follow what is clear to you in this Book.’ ʿUmar said: What is clear, follow; what is not, leave it.

x: Others said fodder means fresh fruit.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: who explained fodder as fresh fruit.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘As provision for you’: We caused these things that the children of Adam eat to grow as provision for you people, for your enjoyment and benefit, and what livestock eat as provision for your livestock. The basic meaning of anʿām is camels, but the word is also used for all grazing animals.
The interpreters said as we have.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah;
m: and he said: Yūnus related to us, from al-Ḥasan, concerning ‘as provision for you and your livestock’: the fruit is provision for you, and the grass for your livestock.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Then, when the Deafening Blast comes’: it is said to be one of the names of the Resurrection. I think it derives from the expression ṣākha so-and-so to another’s voice, meaning that he listened to it, though the listener is called muṣīkh. Perhaps the sound itself is ṣākhkh; if so, this name should refer to the blast of the Trumpet.
Among those who said it is one of the names of the Resurrection:

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās,
m: concerning ‘when the Deafening Blast comes’: this is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection; God magnified it and warned His servants of it.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘The day a person flees from his brother’: that is, when the Deafening Blast comes, on the day a person flees from his brother. By ‘flees from his brother,’ it means he flees away from his brother, his mother, and his father… …and his wife, meaning the woman who was his wife in this world, and his children, for fear that they would demand from him what was due between them and him in claims and wrongs.

Some said ‘a person flees from his brother’ means he flees away from his brother so he will not see him and what befalls him. ‘Each person among them’ means the man, his brother, his mother and father, and all the others mentioned in this verse. ‘That day’ is the Day of Resurrection, when the Deafening Blast comes. ‘A matter to occupy him’ means a concern that keeps him occupied and distracts him from anyone else.

c: Bishr related to us, from Yazīd, from Saʿīd, from Qatādah,
m: concerning ‘each of them that day will have a matter to occupy him’: every person will be overtaken by something that distracts him from other people.

c: Abū ʿAmmār al-Marwazī al-Ḥusayn ibn Ḥurayth related to us, from al-Faḍl ibn Mūsā, from ʿĀʾidh ibn Shurayḥ, from Anas, who said:
m: ʿĀʾishah asked the Messenger of God, ‘Messenger of God, may my father and mother be your ransom, I want to ask you about something; tell me what you know.’ He said, ‘If I know about it.’ She asked, ‘Prophet of God, how will the men be gathered?’ He said, ‘Barefoot and naked.’ She waited a while, then asked, ‘How will the women be gathered?’ He said, ‘Likewise, barefoot and naked.’ She said, ‘What a shameful day, the Day of Resurrection!’ He replied, ‘Is that what you are asking about? A verse has been revealed to me that makes it no difference whether you are clothed or not.’ She asked, ‘Which verse, Prophet of God?’ He replied, ‘Each of them that day will have a matter to occupy him.’

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying concerning God’s words, ‘Each of them that day will have a matter to occupy him’: each will have a concern that keeps him from his companion.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Some faces that day will be radiant’: God says that some faces will be bright and shining that day. They are the faces of the believers with whom God is pleased. One says, ‘So-and-so’s face asfara’ when it becomes beautiful; likewise, the dawn asfara when it grows bright. Anything luminous is musfir. Safara without an alif, however, is said of a woman when she removes her veil from her face; one says safarat al-marʾah, ‘the woman unveiled her face.’ Tawbā ibn al-Ḥumayyar said: ‘Whenever I visited Laylā, she veiled herself; but one morning her unveiling aroused my suspicion’—by ‘unveiling’ he means removing the veil from her face. ‘Laughing’ means laughing from joy at the bliss and honor God has given them; ‘rejoicing’ means hopeful for even more.
The interpreters gave a similar explanation of ‘radiant.’

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: it means shining.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying: these are the people of Paradise.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘And some faces that day will be covered with dust’: God says these are the faces of the unbelievers, with dust upon them that day. It is reported that after God judges among the animals and turns them to dust, that dust will become a covering upon the faces of the unbelievers. ‘Veiled by gloom’ means that gloom will envelop those faces; it is dust.
The interpreters said similarly.

c: ʿAlī related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiyah, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said
m: it means humiliation covers them.

c: Yūnus related to me that
m: Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd as saying these are the faces of the people of Hell; qatarah is a kind of dust, and the two are the same. In this world, however, qatarah is what rises up toward the sky and is carried by the wind, while what remains low on the ground is called ghabarah.

x: Regarding His saying, ‘Those are the unbelievers, the wicked’: God, exalted is His mention, says that those described in this way on the Day of Resurrection are people who disbelieved in God and were wicked in their religion in this world. They did not care what acts of disobedience to God they committed or what prohibitions they violated. God will repay them for their evil deeds as He has told His servants. This concludes the commentary on Sūrat ʿAbasa (He Frowned).

notes.en: This is the reading of Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, and ʿĪsā; it is an irregular reading. Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ 8/427.
